01.r: On the day he does the work.
01.n: Literally 'in his day'. The 'his' most likely means the worker's own working day, so the pay falls due the day it is earned; that is a reasonable reading, and several translations make it 'the same day'.

02.r: Pay the worker what he is owed.
02.n: The ordinary verb 'give'; STEP tags it here with the sense 'pay', which the Douay-Rheims and BSB use. The Hebrew has no 'him'.

03.r: The pay he has earned for the day.
03.n: BDB: hire, wages, and also reward for work done. The noun is singular.

04.r: Adds the time limit: before sunset.

05.r: The sun's setting, the end of the working day.
05.n: The verb is the ordinary 'come, go in'; STEP tags it here as the sun's setting, the sun 'going in'. YLT keeps the literal 'go in'.

06.n: Literally 'upon him' or 'upon it'; the Hebrew form serves for both. Most translations take it as the wage; it could also be the worker, and the choice is a matter of reading.

07.r: The sun, marking the end of the day.

08.r: Gives the reason for prompt pay.

09.r: He has nothing laid by to wait on.
09.n: Gesenius: afflicted, wretched, poor. Hebrew has no 'is': literally 'for poor he'.

11.r: Toward the wage, the thing he waits for.
11.n: The phrase stands first for emphasis: it is the wage he is set on.

12.r: The hired man again, written out for emphasis.

13.r: He longs for it and depends on it.
13.n: 'To lift up the soul to' something is a Hebrew idiom for longing for it. Gesenius gives the verb's first sense as TO TAKE UP, TO LIFT UP. A participle: he is always doing it.

14.r: Marks 'his soul' as the object of 'lifts up'.
14.n: This small word marks a definite direct object and has no English equivalent; it is counted here with 'his soul'.

15.r: His whole longing: his living hangs on the wage.
15.n: STEP tags the word here with the sense 'desire'; BDB lists desire and appetite among its senses, alongside soul and life. We keep 'soul' to show the idiom; the KJV and ASV say 'heart', and Geneva and the Douay-Rheims 'life'.

16.r: Warns what will follow if the wage is held back.
16.n: Literally 'and not': 'and he shall not cry out'. The sense is a warning, which English gives as 'lest'; YLT keeps the literal form.

17.r: He calls out to God for justice.
17.n: Gesenius: TO CRY OUT, TO CALL, a word that imitates the sound of crying.

18.r: His complaint is against the employer.
18.n: Literally 'upon you'; with 'cry out' it means against.

20.r: The personal name of Israel's God, who hears the worker.

21.n: A perfect with 'and', carrying the warning forward: 'and it shall be'.

22.r: The guilt rests on the employer.
22.n: The brief's lexicon line for this word ('Punctuation Maqqef') is a data error and is ignored here.

23.r: The withheld wage becomes a sin counted against him.
23.n: Gesenius explains the phrase 'to be sin in someone' as meaning that he is to be reckoned guilty in the matter. The brief's lexicon also gives 'guilt for sin'.

02.n: ἀποδίδωμι, 'give back, render': the payment as something owed.

09.n: πένης, 'a poor man, one who works for his living'.

10.n: ἐστίν, 'is': the Greek turns the Hebrew 'he' into the verb.

13.n: Printed ὦι in our Greek text, which is not a Greek verb; the word is evidently garbled. The sense of the Greek clause is 'and in it he has his hope'.

15.n: ἐλπίς, 'hope': the Greek gives the meaning of the Hebrew idiom, not its picture.

16.n: Printed κα in our Greek text, evidently καί, 'and', cut short. There is no negative here: our Greek reads 'and he will cry out against you'.

19.n: Printed πρὸ in our Greek text; the dictionary form πρός, 'to', fits the sense.
